pr.title: Only assert for child/parent projection compatibility AFTER checking that theyre coming from the same place
pr.description:
This assertion doesn't make sense until we check that these captures are actually equivalent.

Fixes #123697

issues.title: Internal Compiler Error when building an async closure that calls methods on a referenced variable and a cloned referenced variable in a specific order
issues.body:
### Code
This bug only happens when calling a method on two different referenced variables inside an async closure. For some reason, this bug will not happen if the lines are flipped (calling it on test first then temp). It also will not happen if test isn't cloned outside the closure first. 

This will error:
```rust
#![feature(async_closure, async_fn_traits)]

fn main() {}

pub fn test(test: &u64, temp: &u64) {
    let test = test.clone();
    async || {
        temp.abs_diff(12);
        test.clone();
    };
}
```

This will not:
```rust
pub fn test(test: &u64, temp: &u64) {
    async || {
        temp.abs_diff(12);
        test.clone();
    };
}
```

Neither will:
```rust
pub fn test(test: &u64, temp: &u64) {
    let test = test.clone();
    async || {
        test.clone();
        temp.abs_diff(12);
    };
}
```

Nor will:
```rust
pub fn test(test: &u64, temp: &u64) {
    let temp = temp.clone();
    async || {
        test.clone();
        temp.abs_diff(12);
    };
}
```

But if both the order is flipped and the line order is flipped it will crash (variable name changed to make sure shadowing wasn't the issue):
```rust
pub fn test(test: &u64, temp: &u64) {
    let other = test.clone();
    async || {
        temp.clone();
        other.abs_diff(12);
    };
}
```

This setup for the bug was found entirely through trial and error. The original issue was found in a nightly build of a project I'm working on (https://github.com/BigBadE/Raven-Language/actions/runs/8608806965/job/23628381189). 

### Meta
This bug was introduced in the latest version of nightly (2024-04-08). It was not present in 2024-04-07.

rustc 1.79.0-nightly (ab5bda1aa 2024-04-08)

analysis.originalLogic: The StateTransform/ByMoveBody analysis compares a parent coroutine capture with child coroutine captures to derive the child's precise capture projections. Its helper `child_prefix_matches_parent_projections` is a predicate: it reads the parent and child capture bases, then returns true only when `parent_base.var_path.hir_id == child_base.var_path.hir_id` and the zipped projection kinds match. Prefix compatibility (child projection length >= parent projection length) is meaningful only for captures whose bases are the same upvar.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical code performed the projection-length compatibility check too early: it placed `assert!(child_capture.place.projections.len() >= parent_capture.place.projections.len());` unconditionally inside `child_prefix_matches_parent_projections`, before checking that the child and parent came from the same base upvar. Thus a child capture from a different upvar with fewer projections made a predicate that should return false panic instead. The fix moves this assertion to the call site after a matching parent/child capture pair has been selected, guarded by the comment "This analysis only makes sense if the parent capture is a prefix of the child capture."
analysis.inputDomain: Async closures (nightly `async_closure` feature, edition 2021) that capture multiple distinct upvars whose precise capture projection lengths differ, for example one captured reference used through a field (`s.t`, requiring deref+field projections) and another captured reference used directly (`t`, requiring only a deref). Capture order and whether an upvar is cloned/shadowed can change which child capture is inspected first.
analysis.summary: Bug fix in the ByMoveBody portion of StateTransform: an unconditional projection-length assertion was moved out of the capture-matching predicate and applied only after parent/child captures were confirmed to originate from the same upvar. This prevents an ICE when an async closure captures different upvars with different projection lengths.
analysis.trigger: Compiling an async closure that captures at least two different upvars when the child capture being examined has fewer place projections than the parent capture, and the two captures do not share the same base HIR id. The issue reports this when calling methods on two different referenced variables inside the async closure, with a specific capture/use order and with one variable cloned outside the closure.
preconditions: The async_closure feature is enabled on a nightly compiler.
The async closure captures multiple distinct upvars.
The upvars have precise capture projection places of different lengths (for example, field access through a reference versus direct dereference of a reference).
The capture matching code can observe a child capture from a different upvar before or instead of a matching child capture.
pitfalls: Do not place a prefix-length assertion in a predicate/helper that is invoked while scanning candidate captures whose base upvar identity has not yet been established; the helper must be able to return false for unrelated captures.

Prefix compatibility consists of two conditions: same base HIR id and child projection length >= parent projection length. Checking length alone, or checking it before the base identity, is unsound as a predicate invariant.
Zip-based projection comparison alone does not establish a prefix relationship because zip stops at the shorter iterator; length must be checked once identity is known.
Capture ordering and cloning/shadowing alter which captures are seen and in what order, so testing only one source ordering can miss the bug.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a UI `check-pass` test for the async closure case from issue #123697, using edition 2021 and `#![feature(async_closure)]`. Construct an async closure that accesses a field through one referenced upvar and uses a second referenced upvar, e.g. `async || { println!("{}", s.t); println!("{}", t); };`. Vary the ordering of uses and add a variant where one of the references is cloned/shadowed outside the closure, since the issue shows the ordering matters. The regression test should compile successfully rather than triggering the projection-length assertion; no compiler execution is claimed here.
evidence: This bug only happens when calling a method on two different referenced variables inside an async closure.
